title: Didache
subtitle: The teaching of the Lord through the twelve apostles
lead: The Didache ("teaching") is a short church manual from the first generations after the apostles. It opens with "the Two Ways," a lesson on the way of life and the way of death taught to converts before baptism, then gives rules for baptism, fasting and daily prayer (with the Lord's Prayer), prayers over the cup and bread of the church's meal, tests for traveling apostles and prophets, the Sunday gathering, the choosing of overseers and deacons, and a warning about the last days that breaks off in mid-course.

No copy was known until 1875, though a rough reconstruction of some of its features had been made from later books that used it (Lake). That year Philotheos Bryennios found it in a manuscript of 1056 in Constantinople. It is in no Bible among the churches whose canon lists are given below, but it shows how early Christians lived, prayed and organized themselves, and it stands very close to the Gospel of Matthew.
facts: No church among those whose canon lists are given below (Catholic, Reformed, Ethiopian Orthodox). Eusebius (about AD 325) put "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the "rejected writings" (Church History 3.25.4, McGiffert's translation; Greek notha); Athanasius (AD 367) named "the Teaching of the Apostles" among books outside the canon that the Fathers appointed to be read by those newly joining the church (Festal Letter 39).

Unknown. The title credits the teaching to the Lord through the Twelve, but no writer is named. Lake thought the book composite: an older Two Ways, an early church order, and a recension in the surviving manuscript.

Argued. Lake: the original Two Ways "may be early first century or even earlier," the original Teaching "probably early second century, or possibly earlier," and the text of the manuscript "can scarcely be later than the second century." Dates proposed by others run from AD 50-70 (J.-P. Audet) to about 110 (U. Schnelle), with J. A. Draper finding a date before the end of the first century "probable" (as quoted at Early Christian Writings).
Unknown. Most commentators favor Syria or Syro-Palestine; Egypt and Asia Minor have also been proposed (R. A. Kraft, as quoted at Early Christian Writings).
A church order: moral teaching for converts (1-6), rules for worship and church life (7-15) and a warning about the end (16).
16 chapters, 100 verses, with the long title as 1:0.
Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1912), which prints the one complete manuscript, the Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), with "the very few necessary corrections" noted.

Lake names a Latin version of part of the Didache or a related text (two copies), the "Church Ordinances" (KO) and the Apostolic Constitutions book 7, which rewrites the whole. Kraft adds a Greek papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (P.Oxy. 1782, late fourth century, with 1:3b-4a and 2:7b-3:2a), a fifth-century Coptic fragment (10:3b-12:2), a complete Georgian version in a nineteenth-century manuscript (the translation perhaps as early as the fifth century), and an Ethiopic church order that takes in most of 11:3-13:7 and 8:1-2a.
authorship: "The teaching of the Lord through the twelve apostles to the Gentiles" presents the contents as Jesus' teaching handed on by the apostles, not as a book they wrote. Inside, "apostles" are traveling missionaries (11:3-6).

A composite document. Its first part "is always known as 'The Two Ways'"; the whole is "a manual of Church instruction." Whether Barnabas used the Didache, the Didache used Barnabas, or both used a common source "is not clear, but probably the majority of scholars incline to the last view."

Scholars quoted at Early Christian Writings date the book from AD 50-70 (J.-P. Audet) to about 110 (U. Schnelle); J. A. Draper wrote that "A new consensus is emerging for a date c. 100 AD," and A. D. Howell-Smith took chapters 1-6 as a Christian reworking of a Jewish Two Ways. Lake says the book's relation to the original Teaching "may be best studied in Funk's edition of the Didache, and in Harnack's" history of early Christian literature.

audience.to: Gentile converts and the small churches that taught and baptized them: house churches visited by traveling apostles and prophets, praying three times a day, fasting twice a week on days of their own, and beginning to choose their own overseers and deacons. Most commentators place them in Syria or Syro-Palestine (R. A. Kraft, quoted at Early Christian Writings); in 1965 Kraft thought Egypt "somewhat more probable."
audience.why: To give such churches a practical handbook: what to teach a convert before baptism, how to baptize, fast and pray, what to pray at the shared meal, how to tell true visitors from frauds, how to support resident prophets, how to keep Sunday, whom to choose as leaders, and how to wait for the Lord. Knowing it was written for Gentiles living beside Jews explains both its deep Jewish roots and its sharp line against "the hypocrites."
views: The view of most commentators (Audet; Hazelden Walker; Rordorf and Tuilier; Niederwimmer), as R. A. Kraft reports it in the Anchor Bible Dictionary (quoted at Early Christian Writings).
R. A. Kraft (1965) argued for Egypt, as his own dictionary article reports.
Lake reports that many think the Two Ways began as a Jewish pre-Christian lesson for converts, perhaps proselytes, so its first hearers were Gentiles joining Israel.

outline: The way of life: the two great commandments and the sayings of Jesus
My child: small sins and great ones
Teachers, peace, giving and the household
The last days (the text breaks off)

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the Didache as a composite church order: its layers, date and place, its witnesses, and its relation to Matthew and to Barnabas.

lenses.name: Jewish roots
lenses.desc: Reads the book beside Jewish teaching and practice: the Two Ways as a lesson for converts, the meal prayers beside Jewish table blessings, the fast days, prayer three times a day, firstfruits, and the line drawn against "the hypocrites."

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Reads the Didache beside the New Testament, above all Matthew: the sayings of 1:3-5, the Lord's Prayer, the apostles and prophets of Acts and 1 Corinthians, the overseers and deacons of Philippians and 1 Timothy, Matthew 24 in chapter 16.

lenses.name: Worship and church order
lenses.desc: Asks what each practice was (baptism, fasting, the meal, confession, choosing leaders) and points to how today's churches use the Didache, through the site's "Where Christians differ" cards, without ranking them.

sections.b: Early Christian writers mention a book called the Teaching (or Teachings) of the Apostles, but it was thought lost. Lake: it "was not known to be extant until Bryennios in 1875 discovered it in the Patriarchal library of Jerusalem at Constantinople, in the manuscript which also contains I and II Clement." That manuscript, called C (Codex Constantinopolitanus; Kraft calls it H, Codex Hierosolymitanus), is dated to 1056; Bryennios published the Didache in 1883 (Kraft). It remains the one complete copy. Lake printed its text "with the very few necessary corrections"; the site's variants show each of them.

Chapters 1-6 share most of their content with the last chapters of the Epistle of Barnabas (Barnabas 18-20). Lake lists three possibilities, Barnabas used the Didache, the Didache used Barnabas, or both used a common source, and says most scholars favored the last, a source "many think" was a Jewish lesson for converts. The Didache's version is the more orderly; it alone has the block of Gospel sayings in 1:3-6. A Latin version of the Two Ways is one of the four witnesses Lake lists. On this site, Barnabas 18-20 uses the Didache's English wherever the Greek is the same.

Chapters 9-10 hold the church's meal prayers, short and full of Jewish images, with the cup before the bread and no words about Jesus' body and blood. Whether they are the Lord's Supper, a fellowship meal or both is the main question about the book (Kraft sets out the views); chapter 14 adds a Sunday "sacrifice" of breaking bread and giving thanks. See the chapter pages for 9, 10 and 14.

The Didache shows churches in change. Traveling apostles and prophets still arrive and must be tested (11-12); prophets who settle receive the firstfruits as "your high priests" (13); and the community is told to choose its own overseers and deacons, who "too perform for you the service of the prophets and teachers" (15:1). No single overseer leads the church, and the word "elder" does not appear.

Chapter 16 gathers the end-time sayings of Matthew 24 and ends with the Lord "coming on the clouds of the sky." The Greek manuscript stops there and leaves the rest of the page blank. Kraft reports that the Georgian version and the Apostolic Constitutions both go on to the final judgment, and his translation follows the Georgian ending ("... to repay each man according to his work, with justice, before all men and angels. Amen."), though he also allows that the Didache may have ended where the Greek does.

sections.h: The Didache in the early church's lists
sections.b: Eusebius, sorting books into accepted, disputed and rejected, put "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the "rejected writings" with the Epistle of Barnabas, the Shepherd and others (Church History 3.25.4, McGiffert's translation in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers; Kraft gives Eusebius's word as notha, "illegitimate"). He gives no reason. Athanasius in his Festal Letter 39 (367) named "that which is called the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Shepherd" among books not in the canon but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those newly joining the church (paragraph 7). So Athanasius valued it for teaching converts, as its own first chapters intend, but not as Scripture. Kraft notes that these writers quote no excerpts, so their "Teaching" cannot be shown to be exactly our text.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the Didache shows a church learning to live without traveling prophets
spec.body: This is my reading, offered as a theory. Chapters 11-15 seem to move in one direction: visiting apostles are limited to a day or two (11:5), prophets who settle are fed (13:1-3), and "if you have no prophet" the firstfruits go to the poor (13:4). Then the community is told to choose overseers and deacons, who perform "the service of the prophets and teachers" and must not be looked down on (15:1-2). Read in order, the chapters look like a church whose charismatic visitors are growing fewer, giving its settled leaders the honor the prophets had. Kraft too sees 15:1-2 as "reflecting the transition from dependence on itinerant ministers, some of whom have settled (13: 1-2), to indigenous leaders"; what is mine is reading chapters 11-15 in order as one movement.

prompts: A hand-drawn sketch on an old scroll: a teacher and a young learner stand where a path splits in two, one path rising through olive trees into morning light, the other sinking into shadow among broken idols; Greek letters for 'life' and 'death' faintly written beside each path; soft ink washes, cave-drawing figures mixed with modern line art, ragged edges, no hard frame.

A soft sketch on parchment: a small group by a running stream in hill country, one person pouring water three times over a kneeling convert's head while others stand fasting and praying; a clay jar nearby; loose ink lines and earth tones, ancient manuscript style, faded edges.

A sketch on an old scroll: grain growing on many mountains, flowing in faint lines toward a single round loaf on a table beside a cup, with a circle of simple figures gathered around; the words 'from the ends of the earth' in faded Greek letters; soft-edged, hand-drawn, mixing early Christian catacomb art with modern line drawing.

canon.summary: An early Christian church manual, its date argued (Lake: the original Teaching "probably early second century, or possibly earlier"). It is in no Bible among the churches whose lists are given below; Athanasius (367) set it outside the canon but among books for teaching new believers.
accepted_by: Not in the Bible. The Catechism's list of the canon (paragraph 120) gives 46 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books, ending with Revelation; the Didache is not among them.
Not in the Bible. The Westminster Confession lists the 27 New Testament books as "given by inspiration of God" (1.2) and names no other early Christian writing.

Not in the Bible. The church's "Holy Scriptures" page (its Sunday School Department, Mahibere Kidusan) lists 46 Old Testament and 35 New Testament books and places "The Didache and Abthulis" among "Books on Church administration and on counseling," outside those lists. Its New Testament list does include a church order called the Didascalia.

Counted "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the "rejected writings," with the Epistle of Barnabas (Church History 3.25.4, McGiffert's translation; Greek notha, "illegitimate," as Kraft gives it), with no reason given.
Named "the Teaching of the Apostles" among books not in the canon but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those newly joining the church for instruction (Festal Letter 39.7).

provenance.b: The complete Greek text survives in one manuscript, Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), copied in 1056 and found by Bryennios in 1875. Lake lists three other witnesses to the original Teaching: a Latin version of part of the Didache or a related text, the "Church Ordinances" (KO), and the Apostolic Constitutions book 7, and he says their relations "are not clear." Kraft adds a late fourth-century Greek papyrus (P.Oxy. 1782), a fifth-century Coptic fragment, a complete Georgian version and an Ethiopic church order that takes in part of the book.

Lake: "the Didache or 'Teaching' was itself a composite document." The Two Ways (1-6) is shared with Barnabas 18-20; the rules for worship and church life (7-15) have no parallel in Barnabas; the ending (16) draws on Matthew 24. Lake dates the original Two Ways "early first century or even earlier" and the text of C to no later than the second century, "though it is possible that a few phrases in C may represent textual accretions."

rejected_why.h: No reason given in the early lists
rejected_why.b:
Eusebius lists "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the "rejected writings" (Church History 3.25.4, McGiffert's translation; Kraft gives Eusebius's Greek as notha, "illegitimate") and gives no reason for this book. Athanasius sets "the Teaching of the Apostles" outside the canon but among books for new believers (Festal Letter 39.7), again without a reason. Kraft notes that neither quotes the book, so it is not certain they meant our text.

Claude's analysis: a likely reason is the title itself. The book claims the Twelve's teaching but names no apostle as writer, and nothing in it ties it to one. Since its date is argued, this is an inference, not a reason any early writer states.

Athanasius drew the line plainly: books like the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd were "not in the Canon" but appointed to be read by new believers. The book's material lived on in later church orders: Kraft lists the Apostolic Constitutions book 7, which reworks it, and the Ethiopic church order that takes in most of Didache 11:3-13:7 and 8:1-2a.

cited_in.b: The Didache gives the Lord's Prayer in nearly Matthew's form, with a short doxology. Whether it used Matthew's Gospel or the same tradition is argued; the New Testament does not quote the Didache.
The two ways of life and death stand behind Jesus' narrow and wide roads and the Didache's opening; both draw on Deuteronomy 30:15-19 and Jeremiah 21:8.
The Didache's baptismal words are Matthew's exactly.
"Do not give what is holy to the dogs" is quoted as the Lord's word and applied to the meal.
Both keep the Aramaic prayer "Marana tha" in Greek-speaking churches.
Both forbid food sacrificed to idols to Gentile believers.
Chapter 16 follows the end-time sayings of Matthew 24 closely.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how Christians lived and worshiped in the generations after the apostles, the Didache is among the most valuable writings we have: it is early, practical, and shows baptism, fasting, prayer, the meal, ministry and hope as a working church knew them. As a text it rests on a single complete Greek manuscript of 1056, with a complete Georgian version, a few small fragments and later rewritings, so some readings are uncertain, though Lake needed only a handful of corrections. It makes few historical claims beyond its title, which presents apostolic teaching rather than apostolic authorship. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with the New Testament on almost every point, goes beyond it in fixing practices (days, water, prayers) the New Testament leaves open, and in a few places stands in tension with it.

sections.h: 1. A witness to early Christian life: very high
sections.b: It shows a great deal of ordinary church practice in a few pages: what converts were taught, how they were baptized, when they fasted and prayed, what they prayed over bread and cup, how they handled visiting preachers, and how they chose leaders. Its Jewish customs and its simple ministry look early, though Kraft argues the form we have may be no earlier than the mid-second century and that church manuals kept old material long; the practices it shows are old even if the last editing is later.

The whole Greek text is known from C (1056) alone; Kraft lists a complete Georgian version, a Greek papyrus fragment and a Coptic fragment. Lake corrected C in only a few places (9:4, 10:4, 11:5, 14:1; see the variants), and the Latin, the Church Ordinances and the Apostolic Constitutions allow checking in parts. Where the witnesses differ, as at 10:6 ("God," "house" or "Son" of David), C is one witness among several, and the ending after 16:8 is known only from the Georgian version and the Apostolic Constitutions.

The book claims little: its title says the teaching is the Lord's "through the twelve apostles," which can be read as a claim about the source of the teaching, not a statement that the Twelve wrote it. It reports no miracles. Its picture of church life fits what Acts and Paul show of apostles, prophets, overseers and deacons.

Matches: the two great commandments, the sayings of the Sermon on the Mount, the threefold name in baptism, the Lord's Prayer, the coming of the Lord on the clouds. Goes beyond: it fixes Wednesday and Friday fasts, prayer three times a day, a preference for running water, pouring as a fallback, and written meal prayers, all of which the New Testament leaves open. In tension: calling the testing of a prophet speaking in the Spirit the unforgivable sin (11:7) sits uneasily with "Put the spirits to the test" (1 John 4:1) and 1 Corinthians 14:29; the sharp word "hypocrites" (8:1) applies Jesus' warning to a group, read as Jews (Kraft: Pharisees or practicing Jews) or as Christians who kept Jewish days; and giving "as ransom for your sins" (4:6) can be read as conflicting with forgiveness by grace through faith, or alongside Tobit and Daniel without conflict (the site's cards at Proverbs 16 and Tobit 4). The churches' cards cited on the chapter pages set out these readings.

how_to_read.h: As a manual, not a treatise
how_to_read.b: Read the Didache as instructions for a real church: short, practical, sometimes allowing exceptions ("if you cannot ... do what you can"). It does not explain its rules at length, so read the New Testament passages behind them alongside.

how_to_read.h: Beside Matthew and the Old Testament
how_to_read.b: Most of its teaching has a Gospel or Old Testament source; the notes give them. Where it differs from the Gospels, it shows how the sayings of Jesus were taught and prayed before and alongside the written Gospels.

how_to_read.h: As a window, not a rule
how_to_read.b: Churches today appeal to the Didache in their debates about baptism, the Lord's Supper, Sunday and ministry. It shows what one early community did; whether that binds later churches is the question each tradition answers for itself, and the site's cards set out their answers side by side.
